title: Recovery, distributed databases and NoSQL
subtitle: What to do when the power fails mid-transaction — and what changes when data lives on many machines.

sections.title: Failures
sections.body: Transaction failure (a logical error, or deadlock-abort), system crash (memory lost, disk intact) and disk failure (data lost). Recovery must restore atomicity and durability: undo the partial work of uncommitted transactions and redo committed work that had not reached disk.

questions.prompt: After a crash, committed changes that were only in memory must be…

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The log on stable storage records them.

sections.title: Log-based recovery
sections.body: The log records every change as <T, item, old value, new value> plus <T start>, <T commit>. The write-ahead rule: the log record reaches stable storage before the changed data page. After a crash: redo every transaction with a commit record; undo every transaction that started but did not commit, using old values. A checkpoint limits how far back the log must be scanned.

worked.why: Log after a crash: <T1 start>, <T1, A, 50, 70>, <T1 commit>, <T2 start>, <T2, B, 10, 99>. No T2 commit.
T1 committed → redo: A = 70. T2 did not commit → undo: B = 10.

choices.text: Data is written before the log.
The log record is on stable storage before the data it describes.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Otherwise recovery could not undo the change.

figures.caption: Figure 8.2.1 — write-ahead logging
figures.note: The log goes first; the page can wait.
figures.script:
diagram("mode: sequence
[Transaction] as t
[Log on disk] as l
[Data page in buffer] as d
t -> l : <T1, A, 1000, 950>
t -> d : write A = 950 (in memory)
t -> l : <T1 commit>
l --> t : commit acknowledged
d -> d : page flushed to disk later");

problems.prompt: Why must the log record be written before the data page?
problems.answer: If the page reached disk first and the system crashed, the database would contain a change with no record of its old value, making it impossible to undo for an uncommitted transaction.

sections.title: Shadow paging and remote backup
sections.body: Shadow paging keeps two page tables: the current one (modified) and the shadow (untouched). Commit atomically switches the pointer to the current table; a crash simply keeps the old one, so no log is needed — but copying pages fragments storage. For disasters, remote backup ships the log to a standby site for high availability.

choices.text: A single atomic switch of the page-table pointer at commit.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Before it the old state is fully intact.

sections.title: Object-oriented and distributed databases
sections.body: Object databases store objects with identity, inheritance and methods directly. A distributed database spreads data over sites: fragmentation splits a table by rows or columns, replication keeps copies for speed and availability. Transactions across sites use two-phase commit: the coordinator asks all participants to prepare (vote), and only if every one says yes does it tell them to commit.

questions.prompt: In two-phase commit, when does the coordinator decide to commit?

choices.text: Only when every participant voted YES.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: One NO (or timeout) means global abort.

figures.caption: Figure 9.1.1 — two-phase commit
figures.script:
diagram("mode: sequence
[Coordinator] as c
[Site 1] as a
[Site 2] as b
c -> a : PREPARE
c -> b : PREPARE
a --> c : VOTE YES
b --> c : VOTE YES
c -> a : COMMIT
c -> b : COMMIT
a --> c : ACK
b --> c : ACK");

sections.title: Data warehousing and OLAP
sections.body: OLTP systems handle many small transactions; a data warehouse collects historical data from many sources (via ETL: extract, transform, load) for analysis. OLAP views data as a cube of dimensions (time, product, region) and measures (sales), with operations like roll-up, drill-down, slice and dice.

choices.text: Aggregating to a coarser level, e.g. from months to years.

sections.title: NoSQL and big data
sections.body: NoSQL systems trade some relational guarantees for scale and flexibility: key–value stores (Redis), document stores (MongoDB), column-family stores (Cassandra), graph databases (Neo4j). They favour horizontal scaling and flexible schemas. The CAP theorem says a distributed store cannot have Consistency, Availability and Partition tolerance all at once; many choose eventual consistency. Big data: volume, velocity, variety.

questions.prompt: CAP theorem: during a network partition a distributed system must choose between…

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: You cannot give up partition tolerance in practice.

problems.prompt: When would you choose a document store over a relational database?
problems.answer: When records are naturally nested and their shape varies (product catalogues, user profiles), schemas change often, and horizontal scaling matters more than multi-table joins and strict transactions.
